newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - BNP to open with 'vanilla banking' in NZ.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - BNP to open with 'vanilla banking' in NZ.

text.p: Banque Nationale de Paris would launch in New Zealand with "plain vanilla banking" and add the "chocolate sauce" of more exotic activities later, New Zealand Manager Michael Sanders said on Monday.
The French bank, one of the world's top 20 by assets and shareholders' funds, was granted a bank registration by the central Reserve Bank on Friday.
"We will start off with essentially with what you would call the 'plain vanilla' banking services -- loans and guarantees, foreign exchange and money market activities.

"As we build up our domestic client base, because we now have the capacity to deal in New Zealand dollars, we can start adding the chocolate sauce -- funds management, equities and more exotic derivatives and other structured financing transactions," Sanders told Reuters in a telephone interview.
BNP joins a growing list of prominent banking names that have joined a banking scene here now populated with 18 banks, all but one foreign-owned.
Last year, two of the world's biggest names in banking, Deutsche Bank A.G. and Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, as well as agricultural specialist bank Rabobank of the Netherlands, gained registration.
Sanders said BNP was unfazed by an overcrowded market.

"We are sort of used to competition. I think most banking markets are somewhat overcrowded these days but wherever we are, we compete against a wide diversity of competitors and, we like to think, fairly successfully," he said
BNP will not participate in retail banking but specialise in corporate and wholesale banking. With its New Zealand base in Auckland, it wants to build on its extensive regional network.
BNP will operate as a branch so it will be able to bring the full muscle of its NZ$500 billion of assets behind it.
Sanders said BNP would have the capacity to do deals with "substantial money behind us".
"Our focus is on the major corporations -- global corporations, New Zealand corporations on the larger size and State-Owned Enterprises," he said.
Recently BNP's Santiago branch reported a number of New Zealand corporates were seeking opportunities in Chile and BNP wants to help introduce those companies there.
"That would be an example of the global networking that we have," Sanders said. "Traditionally, we have a very strong relationship philosophy, we are not specifically deal-doers."
BNP will do one-off deals but it sees long-term relationships as more important.
In wholesale banking, BNP will concentrate initially on money market activities, where it will be a price maker, and later hopes to be a forex price maker "in the fullness of time".
Sanders said BNP will begin as a "fairly lean" operation with a principal focus on business development. Future size would depend on how well the market developed.
He said BNP's registration was a vote of confidence in the New Zealand economy, where radical economic reforms of the last decade had been followed closely.
"New Zealand is an example to many countries. You are looking

at a stable economy, stable politics, a very simple tax system that looks very effective, an outward-looking economy. There are a lot of very positive things about the New Zealand economy which appeal."

With a banker's tact, Sanders declined to comment on whether the healing of the rift between Paris and Wellington over French nuclear testing in the South Pacific in 1995 had cleared the way for BNP to register. He said, however, that the timing was good. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
